## Introduction

And now folks, we get down to it. The piece de resistance of 21st century statistics: neural networks.

I have debated long and hard on how to present this topic. As a mathematician, I like theory and there is A LOT of linear algebra going on under the hood, but I don't want to get caught up in those details^[I'll try to write a supplement later.]. So let's not start there. 

There are A LOT of predefined functions and workflows. We could just learn them and be done with it. But then you don't get any insights beyond the black box so I don't really want to start there either. 

Short of outsourcing this to 3Blue1Brown's Deep Learning series (which I do highly recommend you watch), the starting place I have decided on is decision boundaries for classification problems. We talked about this topic back in Module 3 with logistic regression so we'll begin with a review of what type of decision boundaries arise in such models and then discuss when they fail.  

## Linear Decision Boundary

As usual, we'll begin with some fake data generated in the following way

- Class A observations have two independent features $X_1, X_2$, both drawn from a normal distribution with mean -1 and std.dev =1
- Class B observations have two independent features $X_1, X_2$, both drawn from a normal distribution with  mean 1 and std.dev =1

The following code generates 250 observations for each class:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(1015)
class_colors = c("A" = "#E35205", "B" = "#004080")

n_per_class = 250
sd = 1
fake_data=rbind(
    data.frame(
      x1 = rnorm(n_per_class, -1, sd),
      x2 = rnorm(n_per_class, -1, sd),
      class = "A"
    ),
    data.frame(
      x1 = rnorm(n_per_class, 1, sd),
      x2 = rnorm(n_per_class, 1, sd),
      class = "B"
    ) 
  )|>
    mutate(class = factor(class, levels = c("A", "B")))

ggplot(fake_data, aes(x1, x2, color = class)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = class_colors) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    x = "X1",
    y = "X2",
    color = "Class"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Notice that in this case, the boundary between the two classes, though blurred in many ways, is basically linear; I could draw a line which would roughly separate the two clusters. This line can be found using logistic regression as in Module 3: 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fake_glm = glm(
  class ~ x1 + x2,
  data = fake_data,
  family = binomial
)

summary(fake_glm)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

Call:
glm(formula = class ~ x1 + x2, family = binomial, data = fake_data)

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept) -0.06186    0.18660  -0.332     0.74    
x1           2.00903    0.23481   8.556   <2e-16 ***
x2           2.04204    0.23714   8.611   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 693.15  on 499  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 191.10  on 497  degrees of freedom
AIC: 197.1

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 7
```


:::
:::


Note that the "positive" class is B; the logistic model spits out the probability that an observation fits into this class.  We classify an observation as B when its estimated probability exceeds 0.5, and as A otherwise. We can plot the decision boundary using code similar^[Exception: switched to geom_raster here for a nicer way to fill the regions. Also turning it into a function for duplicate use] to what we did in Section 3.2: 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot_boundary=function(model,data){
  grid = expand_grid(
      x1 = seq(min(data$x1) - 0.5, max(data$x1) + 0.5,
             length.out = 250),
      x2 = seq(min(data$x2) - 0.5, max(data$x2) + 0.5,
             length.out = 250)
    )

  preds=predict(model, newdata = grid, type = "response")
  grid$pred_class = if_else(preds > 0.5, "B", "A")
  grid = grid |>
      mutate(pred_class = factor(pred_class, levels = c("A", "B")))

  ggplot() +
    geom_raster(
      data = grid,
      aes(x1, x2, fill = pred_class),
      alpha = 0.2
    ) +
    geom_point(
      data = data,
      aes(x1, x2, color = class),
      alpha = 0.7
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = class_colors) +
    scale_color_manual(values = class_colors) +
    coord_equal() +
    labs(
      x = "X1",
      y = "X2",
      color = "Observed class",
      fill = "Predicted class"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}
plot_boundary(fake_glm,fake_data)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::

The background colors show the predicted class. The boundary between the two regions is where the model assigns probability 0.5 to Class B and as we showed in Module 3, is given by the equation of a line. 

Because of this, the predictive accuracy of our model will be strong. To demonstrate, let's do a training-testing split and calculate predictions on the test set:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
n=nrow(fake_data)
s=sample(n,0.7*n)
train=fake_data[s,]
test=fake_data[-s,]

train_glm = glm(
  class ~ x1 + x2,
  data = train,
  family = binomial
)

calculate_accuracy=function(model,data){
  y=data$class
  preds=predict(model,data,type="response")
  yhat= ifelse(preds>0.5,"B","A")
  cat("Accuracy:",sum(yhat==y)/nrow(data))
}

calculate_accuracy(train_glm,test)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Accuracy: 0.9066667
```


:::
:::


Not too shabby. 


## Nonlinear decision boundary. 

Now to create a more challenging problem. This time, Class A observations lie inside a disk centered at the origin, while Class B observations lie in a surrounding ring^[Not gonna lie, outsourced the code for this one to chatGPT.]. The classes are separated by a circular boundary rather than a straight line:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
n_per_class = 250
inner_radius = 1
ring_inner = 1.15
ring_outer = 2.5 

make_disk = function(n, r_min, r_max, label) {
    angle = runif(n, 0, 2 * pi)
    radius = sqrt(runif(n, r_min^2, r_max^2))

    data.frame(
      x1 = radius * cos(angle),
      x2 = radius * sin(angle),
      class = label
    )
  }

disk_data=bind_rows(
  make_disk(n_per_class, 0, inner_radius, "A"),
  make_disk(n_per_class, ring_inner, ring_outer, "B")
) |>
  mutate(class = factor(class, levels = c("A", "B")))


ggplot(disk_data, aes(x1, x2, color = class)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_manual(values = class_colors) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(
    x = "X1",
    y = "X2",
    color = "Class"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Let's try and refit a logistic model to our data and look at both the decision boundary:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
n=nrow(fake_data)
s=sample(n,0.7*n)
disk_train=disk_data[s,]
disk_test=disk_data[-s,]


disk_glm = glm(
  class ~ x1 + x2,
  data = disk_train,
  family = binomial
)

plot_boundary(disk_glm,disk_train)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


and accuracy:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
calculate_accuracy(disk_glm,test)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Accuracy: 0.6466667
```


:::
:::


Now that's shitty! 

The reason is that logistic regression cannot enclose the inner disk with a straight line. This is not just a problem in how we estimated coefficients,its a limitation of the model structure^[Hold your head up high logistic, we still love you. Everyone has their limits.].  

## How do we fix it? 

Well, knowing that the problem is circular, we could engineer a new variable representing distance from the origin:  

$$
r = \sqrt{X_1^2 + X_2^2}
$$

Let's take a look at logistic regression with this feature explicitly thrown in there: 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
disk_train = disk_train |>
  mutate(r = sqrt(x1^2 + x2^2))

disk_test = disk_test |>
  mutate(r = sqrt(x1^2 + x2^2))

disk_glm_radius = glm(
  class ~ r,
  data = disk_train,
  family = binomial
)

plot_radius_boundary = function(model,data) {
  grid = expand_grid(
    x1 = seq(min(data$x1) - 0.5, max(data$x1) + 0.5,
             length.out = 250),
    x2 = seq(min(data$x2) - 0.5, max(data$x2) + 0.5,
             length.out = 250)
  ) |>
    mutate(r = sqrt(x1^2 + x2^2))

  grid$p_B = predict(model, newdata = grid, type = "response")
  grid$pred = factor(
    if_else(grid$p_B > 0.5, "B", "A"),
    levels = c("A", "B")
  )

  ggplot() +
    geom_raster(
      data = grid,
      aes(x1, x2, fill = pred),
      alpha = 0.2
    ) +
    geom_contour(
      data = grid,
      aes(x1, x2, z = p_B),
      breaks = 0.5,
      color = "black",
      linewidth = 1
    ) +
    geom_point(
      data = data,
      aes(x1, x2, color = class),
      alpha = 0.7
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = class_colors) +
    scale_color_manual(values = class_colors) +
    coord_equal() +
    labs(
      title = "Classification boundary from the radius model",
      x = "X1",
      y = "X2",
      fill = "Predicted class",
      color = "Observed class"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}

plot_radius_boundary(disk_glm_radius,disk_train)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
calculate_accuracy(disk_glm_radius,disk_test)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Accuracy: 1
```


:::
:::


That is quite an improvement in accuracy! This model can learn a circular decision boundary because the squared-distance feature is nonlinear in the original predictors.

## Where neural networks come in...

The issue is that with real data, you might not be able to see a clear circular structure like you can in this fake example and instead need your algorithm to find it for you. That's where a neural network helps us out. Instead of manually constructing a squared-distance feature, we let the model learn intermediate features from the original predictors.

A neural network contains a series of layers^[The type of neural network we describe here is a type of feedforward neural network called a multiplayer perceptron. And yes, I do think they should name a Transfomer that.] First, the input layer consists of the inputs (i.e., features) that we give the model. Next, a hidden layer consists of hidden units that learn patterns in the data. Each hidden unit takes a weighted sum of the inputs and passes it through a function called an activation function. For example, a logistic (sigmoid) function can serve as an activation function, although many modern neural networks use the ReLU function instead. In this way, the network engineers its own features in the hidden layer and passes these learned features to an output layer, which uses them to make the final predictions. The diagram below illustrates this architecture:

![Architecture of a neural network](nnet.jfif){fig-align="center" width="60%" fig-cap="Architecture of a neural network."}

The `nnet` package in R contains some basic features for fitting neural networks to data. We'll start with 8 hidden units (`size = 8`):


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(nnet)
disk_nn = nnet(
  class ~ x1 + x2,
  data = disk_train,
  size = 8,
  trace=FALSE
)
```
:::


The `trace=FALSE` just suppresses the output showing the iterations. The hidden units combine the original predictors using learned weights and apply nonlinear activation functions. The output layer uses these learned features to predict the class.

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
plot_boundary_nn=function(model,data){
  grid = expand_grid(
      x1 = seq(min(data$x1) - 0.5, max(data$x1) + 0.5,
             length.out = 250),
      x2 = seq(min(data$x2) - 0.5, max(data$x2) + 0.5,
             length.out = 250)
    )

  grid$pred_class = predict(model, grid, type = "class")
  grid = grid |>
      mutate(pred_class = factor(pred_class, levels = c("A", "B")))

  ggplot() +
    geom_raster(
      data = grid,
      aes(x1, x2, fill = pred_class),
      alpha = 0.2
    ) +
    geom_point(
      data = data,
      aes(x1, x2, color = class),
      alpha = 0.7
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = class_colors) +
    scale_color_manual(values = class_colors) +
    coord_equal() +
    labs(
      x = "X1",
      y = "X2",
      color = "Observed class",
      fill = "Predicted class"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
}
plot_boundary_nn(
  disk_nn, 
  disk_train
) 
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Unlike logistic regression on the original predictors, the neural network learned the nonlinear decision boundary all by its own self. It even gets close to 100% accuracy. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
y=disk_test$class
yhat= predict(disk_nn,disk_test,type="class")
cat("Accuracy:",sum(yhat==y)/nrow(disk_test))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Accuracy: 0.9933333
```


:::
:::

Slow...clap. 

## Experimenting with the network architecture

There are a number of hyperparameters hidden underneath the hood a neural network, but one of the most transparent is `size`. Using `size = 0` would be equivalent to fitting a logistic regression model^[Although this choice is not supported by the function `nnet`.] (no hidden units). The graphs below demonstrate how the decision boundary depends on this parameter in our example:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
fit_network = function(size, data) {
  nnet(
    class ~ x1 + x2,
    data = data,
    size = size,
    trace=FALSE
  )
}

nn_2 = fit_network(2, disk_train)
nn_4 = fit_network(4, disk_train)
nn_8 = fit_network(8, disk_train)
nn_16 = fit_network(16, disk_train)

plot_boundary_nn(nn_2,disk_train) +
  labs(title="Size = 2")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
plot_boundary_nn(nn_4,disk_train) +
  labs(title="Size = 4")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-2.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
plot_boundary_nn(nn_8,disk_train) +
  labs(title="Size = 8")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-3.png){width=672}
:::

```{.r .cell-code}
plot_boundary_nn(nn_16,disk_train) +
  labs(title="Size = 16")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](notes2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-4.png){width=672}
:::
:::


You can see how the learning of the circular boundary shape improves with the number of hidden units in this example. However, I would be cautious about using too many hidden units in general because of the potential for overfitting. The bias-variance tradeoff still applies (larger size, higher bias)! 

## A real data example

Neural networks (like random forests, trees, and gradient boosting) can be applied to both classification and regressions problem, but since the examples above are all in the classification setting, we'll start there with our water polo dataset:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df_url="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jmayberr/math133-stat-learning-fall2026/refs/heads/main/Datasets/womenShots.csv"
shots=read.csv(df_url) %>%
  select(-X.1,-X,-start.time,-end.time,-category)
formula=Goal~Tactic+Type+Hand+Defense+distance+abs(angle)
glimpse(shots)
```

The fit can get even better with variable scaling as illustrated in the example and practice problems below. 

## Regression Example

Neural networks can be applied to regression problems as well. To illustrate, we'll throw `nnet` at our favorite old election dataset


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
df_url="https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jmayberr/math133-stat-learning-fall2026/refs/heads/main/Datasets/election2016.csv"
election2016=read.csv(df_url)
s=sample(50,30)
train=election2016[s,]
test=election2016[-s,]
```
:::


The one change we need to make is set `linout=TRUE` to specify a numeric response^[Technically, the `linout` is telling it to use the identify function for the output function as opposed to a logistic or softmax; see the supplement for details.]. We'll only use four hidden units because the size of our training set is so small. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
trump_nn=nnet(trump.vote~.,
              data=train[,2:10],
              size=4,
              linout=TRUE,
              trace=FALSE)
```
:::


Let's see how well the predictions do on our test set based on RMSE


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
yhat=predict(trump_nn,newdata=test)
sqrt(mean((yhat-test$trump.vote)^2))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.1169145
```


:::
:::


Interestingly, this is worse than many simpler models we considered and doesn't see to get better if we increase the number of hidden units. 

One reason for that is variable scaling. Neural networks are sensitive to such things just like shrinkage. If we instead scale the variables first,


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
election_scaled=election2016 |>
  mutate(across(median.income:non.white,~ as.numeric(scale(.x))))
s=sample(50,30)
train=election2016[s,]
test=election2016[-s,]
```
:::


The predictions improve a little. 


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
nn_test=nnet(trump.vote~.,
              data=train[,2:10],
              size=4,
              linout=TRUE,
              trace=FALSE)
yhat=predict(nn_test,newdata=test)
sqrt(mean((yhat-test$trump.vote)^2))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.09964994
```


:::
:::

The difference is even more drastic in the practice problems below.
